lesson.title: Comparison of Economic Exchange
lesson.summary: A method for comparing the Silk Roads, Indian Ocean, and trans-Saharan networks with specific evidence and explained reasoning.
learningGoals: Compare similarities and differences among the three major exchange networks.
Support a comparison with specific, relevant evidence from at least two networks.
Explain how geography, technology, state power, and cultural exchange shaped different outcomes.
lesson.bigIdea: All three networks connected producers and consumers and depended on political and environmental conditions, but their routes, technologies, goods, and state structures produced meaningful differences.
lesson.context: The networks developed from older routes and settlements. The period from 1200 to 1450 intensified exchange across Afro-Eurasia, making comparison useful while still requiring attention to overlap and regional variation.

sections.title: How to compare historically

blocks.text: A comparison begins with a shared category: route geography, transport, commercial practice, state involvement, or cultural consequence. It then identifies a similarity or difference and explains why it existed. Listing one fact about each network is not yet an argument.

For example, all three networks depended on political stability to some degree, but the form of protection differed. A comparison becomes stronger when it names the institution, identifies the mechanism, and explains the result.

Good comparisons also define their limits. Networks overlapped, varied over time, and contained many communities. Treating them as sealed boxes hides the very connections the unit asks students to explain.

sections.takeaway: Comparison requires a common dimension, specific evidence, and a reasoned explanation of the relationship.

sections.title: Shared causes and effects

blocks.text: Demand for goods, agricultural production, commercial knowledge, and state protection helped all three networks grow. Merchants, diplomats, missionaries, and migrants moved along them, and trading cities became important nodes.

All networks spread cultural practices and created opportunities for rulers and merchants. They also carried risk: war, environmental stress, and disease could disrupt exchange. Similar effects do not mean identical experiences or equal benefits.

A defensible shared-cause claim must use more than a vague phrase such as “trade increased.” Explain how a technology, institution, or political decision changed the conditions of exchange in at least two networks.

sections.takeaway: Shared processes are useful only when supported with specific mechanisms and examples.

sections.title: Geography changes the route

blocks.text: The Silk Roads crossed deserts and mountain passes, encouraging caravan travel and exchange in valuable, portable goods. Indian Ocean routes used ships and monsoon timing to connect coastal and island markets. Trans-Saharan routes depended heavily on camel caravans and oases.

These differences affected what was practical. Ships could carry larger or heavier loads than many overland caravans, while desert caravans needed water planning and load-bearing saddles. Neither network was technologically simple; each required specialized knowledge.

A route’s geography also influenced which cities grew. An oasis, river crossing, strait, or deepwater port could become a service node, but political decisions and security determined whether that advantage lasted.

sections.takeaway: Transport and geography shaped what moved, when it moved, and which places became important.

sections.title: States and communities

blocks.text: States supported exchange through protection, taxation, ports, roads, customs, and diplomacy. Mali benefited from West African gold and trade revenue; Malacca gained from its strategic strait; Mongol khanates shaped large portions of overland Eurasia.

Communities also sustained exchange. Diasporic merchants, caravan specialists, sailors, farmers, artisans, and local brokers made networks work. A ruler could claim authority over a route, but everyday expertise remained distributed among many groups.

Cultural outcomes followed these political and social arrangements. Islam, Buddhism, language, architecture, and scientific knowledge circulated through different institutions. Comparison should ask who carried an idea and how local people changed it.

sections.takeaway: Exchange depended on both states and ordinary specialists, whose roles differed by network.

sections.title: From comparison to argument

blocks.text: A thesis should make a defensible claim about degree, cause, or significance. For example: all three networks expanded through political support and specialized transport, but the Indian Ocean’s seasonal maritime system created different port communities than the overland routes.

Evidence must do work. Naming Malacca and Timbuktu shows knowledge; explaining how a strait and a desert city generated different revenue and services supports the comparison. Reasoning connects the example to the claim.

Complex arguments recognize a qualification. A network can be mostly maritime and still rely on inland routes; a state can protect trade and also exploit merchants or conquered people. Nuance is historical accuracy, not indecision.

sections.takeaway: A comparison becomes an argument when evidence is connected to a claim and qualified where the pattern varies.

connections.title: Regional states make the comparison concrete
connections.body: Unit 1 gives background on China, South and Southeast Asia, Africa, and Europe. Topic 2.7 uses that regional knowledge to compare how particular states and communities participated in connected economic systems.
connections.transferQuestion: What evidence would you use to test the relationship described in Regional states make the comparison concrete?
connections.feedback: A strong transfer answer names a concrete example, identifies both sides of the relationship, and explains the mechanism rather than repeating the title.

connections.title: Commercial tools are answers to route problems
connections.body: Topics 2.1–2.4 present credit, caravanserai, ships, monsoon knowledge, camel saddles, and ports. In a comparison, name the problem each tool solved instead of treating technology as a list of inventions.
connections.transferQuestion: What evidence would you use to test the relationship described in Commercial tools are answers to route problems?
connections.feedback: A strong transfer answer names a concrete example, identifies both sides of the relationship, and explains the mechanism rather than repeating the title.

connections.title: Cultural and environmental consequences belong in the argument
connections.body: Topics 2.5 and 2.6 make comparison richer. Networks moved beliefs and knowledge, but also crops, disease, and pressure on land. A strong synthesis explains both connection and uneven outcomes.

glossary.definition: The way terrain, water, winds, distance, and strategic locations shape where exchange can occur and which transport methods are practical.
glossary.sourceLabel: AMSCO Unit 2 Topic 2.7; College Board CED Topic 2.7
glossary.verificationNote: Original definition matches the comparison lesson's shared comparison dimension.

glossary.definition: A repeated way of organizing exchange, such as credit, brokerage, taxation, customs, partnership, or the movement of payment and goods.
glossary.sourceLabel: AMSCO Unit 2 Topic 2.7; College Board CED Topic 2.7
glossary.verificationNote: Original definition is broad enough for comparison but does not replace network-specific evidence.

glossary.definition: A condition in which institutions and authorities provide enough predictable order for people, goods, or information to move, though protection may remain uneven.
glossary.sourceLabel: AMSCO Unit 2 Topic 2.7; College Board CED Topic 2.7
glossary.verificationNote: Original definition preserves the comparison lesson's qualification that political protection differed by network and period.

glossary.definition: The ways governments shape exchange through protection, taxation, roads, ports, customs, diplomacy, administration, or deliberate redirection of routes.
glossary.sourceLabel: AMSCO Unit 2 Topic 2.7; College Board CED Topic 2.7
glossary.verificationNote: Original definition is a comparison tool and does not imply that states controlled every exchange.
